segments.text: In the summer of 1944 in Normandy,
a Canadian general grew tired
of watching his infantry get cut to pieces
before they even reached the German trenches.
The soldiers were not dying primarily
from tank duels or sniper fire.
They were being killed by artillery shells
bursting in the air above the open trucks
and lightly armored half-tracks,
carrying them to the start line.
So Brigadier General Guy Simons ordered mechanics
to take dozens of surplus self-propelled artillery carriages
and old tank hulls, torch off the guns,
rip out the ammunition racks,
and pack infantry benches into the empty steel tubs.
They called the contraption the Kangaroo
and casualties among the troops
riding in them dropped immediately.
The modern armored personnel carrier was born
by taking a combat vehicle and throwing away its gun.
That origin story points straight
to the question this video answers.
Today, every major army fields heavily armed infantry
fighting vehicles alongside main battle tanks.
Why do those same armies still buy tens of thousands
of armored personnel carriers
that mount little more than a machine gun?
And how does an armored box balance carrying a full squad,
moving fast across a country,
and keeping everyone inside alive?
The answer is that a carrier solves a problem
no heavy fighting vehicle can afford to solve.
It moves large numbers of people and equipment
through the zone where unarmored trucks die,
without paying the crippling weight and space penalty
of a heavy turret.
Start with what the armor on a carrier
is actually built to stop.
On any battlefield since the First World War,
the biggest killer of soldiers in transit
has not been the armor-piercing dart of a tank.
It has been high-explosive shell splinters, mortar fragments,
and machine gun fire reaching several commatters
behind the front line.
Stopping a tank round takes tens of tons of composite plate
across the nose.
Stopping steel shell fragments and rifle bullets all around the hull
takes only a centimeter or two of high-hardness steel
or a thicker slab of welded aluminum,
often spaced with a ceramic layer on the outside.
Because the carrier refuses to carry a heavy cannon
and a deep turret basket,
its interior opens up into a clean rectangular cavern.
Where an infantry fighting vehicle squeezes six or eight soldiers
around a central turret ring,
an armored personnel carrier seats nine to 12 riflemen along the walls,
together with their anti-tank missiles,
spare mortar rounds, stretchers, and water cans.
Look at the classic American M113,
which entered service in 1960
and was built in the tens of thousands.
From the outside,
it looks like an aluminum shoebox on tracks.
Yet precisely because it is an empty box
with a big ramp at the back,
an army can pack a whole squad
and a weekend's worth of ammunition into it
and still keep the vehicle light enough
to cross a country bridge.
Getting that box to the fight brings up the next trade,
which is tracks against wheels.
Early carriers like the M113 or the British FV432
ran on steel tracks
so they could follow tanks across deep mud.
Tracks spread weight well,
but they are loud, thirsty, slow on paved highways,
and chew themselves up
if driven hundreds of commiliters on their own.
Moving a tracked battalion across a country
usually means loading every vehicle
onto a fleet of heavy flatbed trucks first.
That bottleneck is why most modern armored personnel carriers,
such as the American Striker, the European Boxer,
the French VBCI, and the Russian BTR family,
ride on eight large driven wheels instead.
An eight-wheeled carrier can roll out of its barracks
onto a highway, cruise at nearly 100 km an hour
for 500 km on its own tires,
and arrive at the front the same evening
using a fraction of the fuel and spare parts
a tracked column would burn.
To keep those wheels from sinking when the pavement ends,
drivers use a central tire inflation system
controlled from the dashboard.
By bleeding air out of all eight tires on the move,
the vehicle flattens its footprint like a snowshoe
to crawl over soft mud or sand,
then pumps the tires hard again once it hits tarmac.
Inside each tire sits a solid rubber ring
attached to the wheel rim,
so even if machine gun fire shreds the outer rubber,
the carrier can still drive out of the ambush
on the inner cores.
Riding higher on wheels creates its own danger,
because roads and tracks are exactly
where an enemy buries mines and improvised bombs.
Older flat-bottomed carriers trap the upward blast
of a mine right against the floor plate,
turning the hull floor into a hammer
underneath the soldier's boots.
Modern wheeled carriers sit high off the ground
and shape their lower hull into a shallow V or double V profile,
deflecting the blast wave and hot gas outward to the sides
instead of taking it square on the belly.
Even the wheel stations are designed to break away cleanly
in a big explosion, carrying part of the blast energy with them
rather than twisting the troop cabin.
Up on the roof, the way a carrier defends itself
has changed for the same reason.
For decades, a machine gunner had to stand in an open hatch
behind a small steel shield, exposed from the chest
up to snipers and shell bursts.
Today, almost every modern carrier bolts a remote weapon station
to the roof. A heavy machine gun or an automatic grenade launcher
sits in a stabilized cradle paired with a day and night thermal camera,
while the gunner sits locked inside the armor below,
aiming on a screen with a joystick.
Many lighter wheeled carriers also fold down a trim board at the nose
and spin twin water jets at the stern to swim across slow rivers
without waiting for a bridge.
While Western designs keep the engine at the front
so troops walk out a wide rear ramp, the Soviet BTR-60, BTR-70, and BTR-80 series
put their engines at the back to help the hull balance in water.
That forced infantry to scramble out through cramped hatches
wedged right between the middle wheels, a piece of battlefield gymnastics
that convinced many soldiers in combat to ride on the roof
rather than inside the armor.
Because a carrier is essentially a protected self-powered room,
it quietly does 12 jobs behind the rifle squads.
Take the benches out of the back and the same hull becomes an armored ambulance,
a mobile command post packed with radios,
a carrier for a heavy 120-millimeter mortar that fires through roof doors,
an engineer vehicle, or an electronic warfare van.
The European Boxer pushes this idea to its logical conclusion.
Its wheeled chassis and driver's cab form a base unit,
while the entire rear troop compartment is a separate mission pod held on by heavy locks.
In less than an hour, a field crane can lift off a troop module
and drop a fully equipped surgical hospital module onto the exact same eight wheels.
There is an old rueful joke among mechanized infantry
that generals always promise before a war that the armored personnel carrier is strictly a battle taxi,
meant to drop the squad off behind a hill and drive away.
And then the moment the shooting starts,
somebody orders the taxi to charge a trench line like a tank.
Whenever a carrier is pushed into a close gunfight against anti-tank rockets without dismounted infantry
screening it, its thin side armor pays the price.
Which brings us to the misconception that follows the armored personnel carrier in every modern conflict.
Whenever footage appears of a light carrier destroyed near the front line,
commentators declare that the battle taxi is obsolete and that every vehicle should have
tank-grade armor and a big turret.
My own reading is the opposite.
The reach of modern drones and precision artillery means there is no longer a safe rear area 10 or 20
kamaladars behind the trenches.
Everything moving within 20 kamaladars of the front, whether it is a fresh rifle squad,
a crate of mortar bombs, a signal team or four wounded soldiers on stretchers,
now has to travel under a rain of fragments and small warheads.
You cannot build 60-ton tanks to haul stretchers and radio masts,
so the humble armored box is needed in more places today than it ever was.
So return to Normandy in 1944 and those mechanics cutting the guns off old artillery hulls to build
the first kangaroos. Every part of a modern carrier, the fragment-proof hull, the turretless cabin,
the eight self-inflating wheels, the v-shaped belly, and the camera-aimed gun on the roof,
answers that same old arithmetic. A soldier who arrives at the trench in a simple steel box
can still fight. A soldier who never arrives at all cannot.
